prize_parts.citation: for integrating formal theory and empirical analysis to show how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged, but my confidence in ranking it above B001 is lower than in round 1. The case for B006 rests on four points. First, the discovery is conceptual and general: constitutions, electoral rules, accountability and state capacity became endogenous objects of analysis, and government stopped being modelled as a benevolent planner. Second, the work joined formal theory to testable predictions, and it has shaped public finance, development and comparative political economy for roughly 25 to 30 years. Third, the credit boundary is defensible. Persson and Tabellini are the core of the constitutions and electoral-rules programme and its synthesis. Besley's state-capacity and political-agency work is a separable, closely related strand, and it is the part that connects most directly to the long-run state-building literature I know best. Fourth, the citation can be worded around the framework and its testable predictions, so it does not depend on settled causal estimates of any particular constitutional effect. I apply the same test to B001 and to B006, which is whether the originating contributions can be identified and credited without arbitrary exclusions. B006 passes that test more cleanly. I do not count the number of colleagues who prefer an entry as evidence of merit, and I do not treat 'overdue' as a reason.
statement.case_against: My reservations are the same as in round 1, and the first is now weightier. (1) The 2024 institutions prize is a neighbour. Even if the discovery is distinct, the Committee could reasonably judge that a second institutions-themed award so soon is not warranted. (2) The cross-country identification of constitutional effects is weaker than the theory, so part of the empirical record is contested. (3) Persson-Tabellini-Besley is a broad field description, and any three names omit comparable contributors. (4) B001 has greater demonstrated reach into policy practice. Colleagues have also made a serious argument that the origin-point trio of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford is separable by role. That argument removes part of the attribution disadvantage I assigned to B001 in round 1. What remains is the exclusion of Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, a mixed post-2021 record, and the question whether the Taylor rule is a scientific contribution or a policy prescription. Whether those residuals outweigh B001's breadth is a close judgement, and I could see it going the other way.

responses.point: Krusell argues for an origin-point criterion in B001. Calvo and Taylor introduced the pricing and contract mechanisms and Woodford built the welfare-based policy framework. Gali, Gertler, Clarida, Christiano and Eichenbaum codified, estimated and extended that structure. He would not move to Gali or Gertler unless the Committee wanted to reward estimation as the discovery.
responses.response: This is the strongest answer to my round-1 attribution concern, and I accept it as a coherent criterion. It also changes how I read B001's attribution problem. Excluding the estimation-side contributors is a principled cut, not an arbitrary one, and I now treat that problem as smaller than I did. Two things keep me from moving B001 ahead. First, the criterion has to be applied evenly across fields. Applied to B006, it supports Persson and Tabellini as originators of the constitutional programme and Besley as originator of the state-capacity strand. Second, within B001 the criterion still treats three different kinds of contribution as equivalent: a pricing device, a contract model with a policy rule, and a normative synthesis. I also repeat my round-1 point that 'overdue' is not merit. Where we differ is how much weight goes to breadth of policy influence against cleanliness of credit. That is a real judgement difference, not a factual dispute.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first and concedes that credit is broader than any trio. He raises the question whether the Taylor rule is a scientific contribution or a policy prescription, and the priority issues involving Fischer and Phelps. He ranks B006 second and flags the 2024 prize as a brake.
responses.response: I take the 2024 concern as seriously as he does, and I answer it as follows. The 2024 prize addressed whether inclusive institutions cause long-run prosperity, using historical evidence. B006 addresses how specific rules inside a polity map into policy and fiscal outcomes, using formal theory and comparative data. That distinction survives even if the cross-country identification is judged weak, because the contribution is the framework and not any single coefficient. If the Committee reads institutions as a single theme already covered, my case weakens and B001 should lead. His priority questions about the Taylor rule, Fischer and Phelps are the kind of unresolved attribution issue that keeps B001 below B006 on my ranking. I regard them as contestable, not disqualifying, and I would accept a Calvo-Taylor-Woodford citation worded around the originating ideas.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 fourth and proposes only Persson and Tabellini, calling the exclusion of Besley a difficult judgement. He also says B006 is a serious fallback if B002 fails.
responses.response: I accept that Persson and Tabellini alone is defensible, and I still prefer the three-name version. I would want the Committee to decide the framing explicitly. If the citation is built around constitutions and electoral rules, Besley's contribution is a second strand and the pair is the cleaner fit. If it is built around how political institutions shape fiscal policy and state capacity, Besley belongs. I prefer the second framing, because it covers the full achievement and ties it to state formation. If Besley's claim is judged hard to separate from the joint work with Persson, I would support the two-person fallback and not oppose it. I also acknowledge that he reports his B002 preference as a disclosed chair position. I do not rank B002 first, mainly because it competes for the same macro slot as B001, and I have not seen evidence that settles its empirical standing.

responses.point: Teorell separates the 2024 prize from B006: the 2024 question was whether institutions cause prosperity, and this programme concerns how rules within a polity change policy choices. He accepts that the theory outruns the identification, but argues that the contribution is the framework and its testable predictions, not any single estimate.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction and with where he puts the contribution. I would add one caution. Because Teorell and I both work near this literature, we may find the distinction more convincing than colleagues in other fields do. For that reason I would not rest it on a claim that the 2024 prize is irrelevant. It is a neighbouring prize, and the Committee has to weigh how neighbouring it is. I also agree with him that Besley's inclusion depends on framing. My own preference is to include him on the ground that the state-capacity strand is independent. I also note that his round-1 conflict note leaves the 'Persson' co-author question unresolved. I am not treating it as a point either for or against B006.

responses.point: Strömberg moved from B015 to B001. He argues that the award rests on the originating ideas (pricing device, contract structure, policy-rule framework) and not on how well estimated DSGE descendants forecast. He says that framing also answers the estimation-side claimants.
responses.response: That is a useful clarification, and it answers part of the chair's question about the post-2021 record. If the discovery is the originating ideas, the inflation-era performance of estimated models is a limit on the descendants, not on the claim. Even so, the record bears on how the citation should be worded. A citation that credited the framework as a working policy model would be exposed to the empirical debate, while one that credited the originating mechanisms would not. I would also apply his standard to B006. The cross-country effect estimates play the same role there that DSGE forecasts play for B001. The originating framework is what a citation would credit, and the effect estimates are contested downstream evidence. He rated B006 a serious alternative with a cleaner trio, and I agree that the choice between B001 and B006 is close.

uncertainties: How far the Committee will treat the 2024 institutions prize as covering B006's territory. If it does, B001 should lead.
Whether the origin-point criterion can be accepted for B001 without conceding that the Taylor rule is a prescription, and whether the Calvo-Taylor-Woodford trio then stands without Gali or Gertler.
Whether Besley's state-capacity strand is separable enough from the joint work with Persson to justify a third laureate. The fallback is Persson and Tabellini.
How much weight the contested cross-country identification of constitutional effects should carry against the framework contribution.
B020 is a distant alternative that colleagues have not engaged with. Its Saez-Zucman attribution and the policy-advocacy dimension of the work are open.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied ballot text and round-1 files. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or adoption figures.
statement.conflict_note: Updated, not adjudicated. I have no documented collaboration or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini, Besley, Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Piketty or Saez in my supplied profile. I disclose field affinity. My work on railroads and political reform with Johannes Lindvall and Alexandra Cermeño, and my work on long-run state building, sits near Besley's state-capacity strand and near the political-economy field, so I guard against rating B006 on familiarity. I am a Lund colleague of Tommy Andersson, and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund. Neither relationship concerns candidate work. Other members refer to Krusell's and Boppart's IIES proximity to Persson. I note those disclosures as reported, with no claim of verification, and do not treat them as bearing on the merits.
